To panhandle means to sit or stand in a public place and ask strangers for money or food, usually because you are very poor or in financial hardship. You offer nothing in return — no goods, no service, no work. You are simply asking, and hoping a passing stranger will choose to give.

The person who panhandles is called a panhandler, and the act itself is called panhandling.

Picture someone sitting on a city sidewalk, holding a torn piece of cardboard that reads "Homeless. Please help." That is panhandling. Or imagine someone standing near a shop entrance, gently asking each person who walks by, "Excuse me, could you spare some change?" That is also panhandling.

It can take two forms. Passive panhandling is when the person simply sits or stands quietly, perhaps with a cup or a sign, without saying a word to anyone — they just wait and hope. Active panhandling is when the person directly approaches strangers and verbally makes the request. Both count as panhandling.

It typically happens in busy public spaces — sidewalks, street corners, outside train stations, near shop entrances, or at traffic lights where a person might approach stopped cars and knock on the window.
What makes it different from similar things

It helps to know what panhandling is not, so you don't confuse it with related activities.

Panhandling vs. begging: These two words mean essentially the same thing in practice, and you can use them interchangeably in most situations. However, "panhandling" is the more neutral, clinical word — it describes the activity without strong judgment. "Begging" can carry a slightly more pitiful or desperate tone. In American English especially, "panhandling" is the standard word used in news reports, laws, and formal writing.

Panhandling vs. busking: A busker performs in public — playing music, doing magic tricks, drawing portraits — and accepts money for that performance. There is an exchange of entertainment. A panhandler offers nothing in exchange. That is the key difference.

Panhandling vs. fundraising: Fundraising is an organized effort, usually on behalf of a charity or cause, to collect donations from the public. It is planned, often permitted, and structured. Panhandling is personal, individual, and informal.
The tone and connotation of the word

"Panhandle" as a verb is considered a neutral to slightly informal word. It describes a real social phenomenon without being cruel or mocking. Journalists, lawmakers, and social workers use it regularly. You would not use it as an insult — it is simply descriptive. For example, a city might pass a law that says "panhandling is prohibited within 10 feet of a bank entrance" — that is a legal, official use of the word.
How to use it in a sentence

• He has been panhandling on that corner for years.
  • She didn't want to panhandle, but she had no other way to afford food that night.
  • The city council debated whether to ban panhandling near the subway stations.
  • He panhandled enough money to afford a bus ticket home.

Notice that the word works just like any regular verb — past tense is panhandled, the continuous form is panhandling, and the doer is a panhandler.

Panhandling implies a degree of vulnerability or desperation. It is not something people typically choose as a preference — it usually reflects a situation of real need. This is worth keeping in mind because it shapes how the word is used in conversation. Saying someone "panhandles" does not imply they are lazy or dishonest; it simply means they are in a situation where asking strangers for help is the option they have.

To panhandle = to ask strangers in a public place for money or food, offering nothing in return, usually out of poverty or necessity. The person doing it is a panhandler. The activity is panhandling. It is a neutral, standard American English word used in everyday life, journalism, and law.
